details: Runner is stateless w.r.t. sessions; each Run looks up session via sessionService, with isolation enforced at storage layer (GORM Transaction + stale-session optimistic concurrency). Single-writer per session semantics prevent state bleed. Live (bidi) sessions are pod-local, requiring sticky sessions.

Each run/arun call creates its own RunContext; Agent is shared but mostly immutable. Concurrent invocations on the same Agent are safe under async; sessions are keyed by session_id and isolated via DB. AgentOS hosts many agents/sessions with no in-process bleeding.

Runtime does not model sessions as first-class. Each BaseAgent has its own memory; if you share an agent across sessions, memory bleeds. No tenant-scoped isolation primitives - you must build per-session topics yourself.

Isolation enforced at OS subprocess boundary: each session is its own claude CLI process with its own cwd, env, JSONL transcript path. State cannot bleed between subprocesses but shared Python tool handlers share closures/globals. No in-process multi-tenant primitive.

State bleeds across tenants if you reuse a single subprocess. The SDK does not enforce isolation - you must spawn one subprocess per (tenant, session). Known concurrency hazard with SDK MCP servers (#122). Subprocess-per-session is the only safe model.

Multiple Crew instances each have their own id/memory/tools, BUT the event bus is a process-wide singleton and hooks are registered globally. A hook for tenant A fires for tenant B too. No (tenant, hook) scoping primitive.

Isolation enforced by context: each Runner.Run seeds a fresh runContext with its own runSession; mutexes guard internal maps. Parallel sub-agents fork/join the context. Risk: shared state outside runSession.Values is not isolated by the framework.

Each request gets a fresh context.Context (Go HTTP convention). Genkit registry is shared but concurrency-safe-for-reads after Init. No shared mutable session state on the Genkit object; sessions stored in your session.Store[S] implementation.

PregelLoop is one Python instance per run; state lives in checkpointer keyed on thread_id. Inside langgraph_api, @auth.on.* filters enforce resource-scoping at the data layer. BaseStore namespaces can be tenant-scoped by convention but not enforced.
Each workflow.run() creates a new Context (unless explicitly resumed). Sessions are isolated by construction. Context.store is a per-context KV with no global sharing.

RequestContext, MessageList, and SaveQueueManager are all per-call/per-thread. Reserved requestContext keys (MASTRA_RESOURCE_ID_KEY, MASTRA_THREAD_ID_KEY) are server-controlled and cannot be spoofed at HTTP layer. Tool authors must avoid module-level mutable state.

AgentSession holds session_id and per-session mutable state shared with providers. Agents are typically singletons, only sessions are per-conversation. .NET AgentSessionStateBag uses concurrent dictionary entries. State bleed only on anti-pattern usage.

Each run() invocation constructs a fresh RunState. RunContext<TContext> carries app context; no shared runtime to bleed across runs. Approvals/usage shared between parent/forked nested contexts, but app context shared by reference.

Isolation per Session instance (session_id bound at store layer) and per RunContextWrapper (fresh dataclass per Runner.run). Approvals are per-RunContextWrapper. Cross-session bleeding not possible inside SDK unless app shares mutable state via TContext.

Fresh RunContext per run, plus a ContextVar _CURRENT_RUN_CONTEXT scoped via set_current_run_context so concurrent runs in same process don't bleed. Toolset.for_run lets a toolset spawn fresh instance per run for state isolation.

Agent state is largely immutable (model, preamble, static_context, hooks). Mutable surface is ToolServerHandle (Arc<RwLock>) shared across uses. Conversation memory is per-session per backend. Per-call PromptRequest clones agent data so concurrent prompts isolated.

Each Agent holds its own messages/state/tool_registry/hooks/locks/metrics. Agent.stream_async uses threading.Lock that throws ConcurrencyException on concurrent invocations of same instance. UNSAFE_REENTRANT mode opt-in. One Agent per session is required.

Agent.invoke acquires a lock and throws ConcurrentInvocationError if called concurrently on same instance. All state (messages, appState, modelState, registries, hooks) is per-instance. Multi-tenant fan-out requires per-request new Agent(...).

No in-process session bag in `ai`; each request has its own JS scope, messages, runtimeContext. No shared mutable state that one tenant could leak to another, provided messages and runtimeContext come from request scope.

Session state externalized to database (or Vertex Agent Engine), so N pods share session pool. Stale-session check prevents lost updates from racing pods. No leader election. Live (bidi) sessions are pod-local requiring sticky sessions.

Stateless workers share session pool via same database (PostgresDb or AsyncPostgresDb). Session keyed by session_id (UUID). No general leader election, but scheduler uses DB-backed leader election via agno_schedules rows and SchedulePoller claiming locks.
Runtime is SingleThreadedRuntime, no leader election, no distributed lock, no shared store. 'N pods serve same session pool' pattern is BYO entirely. No primitives provided.

No leader election, no shared coordinator. SessionStore adapter is the only shared-state primitive, and it is append-only - concurrent writes to same session from two pods would interleave unsafely. SDK assumes one process owns one session at a time. SessionKey.project_key is documented sharding lever.

SessionStore interface plus Postgres adapter (examples/session-stores/postgres/) lets any pod resume any session ID. forkSession is store-aware. No leader election; pods can serve different sessions but not the same session pool without external store.

OSS: no shared state, no leader election, no message-queue support. Two pods running same crew code do not share state (LanceDB/SQLite are local). Externalize memory backend or implement custom checkpoint BaseProvider yourself. AMP solves this by hosting the runtime.

Stateless Go binary scales trivially. For shared state across pods, your CheckPointStore implementation is the seam - point all pods at same Postgres CheckPointStore. Leader election, locking, partition assignment not provided - layer optimistic concurrency on top of your store.

Stateless workers replicate behind Cloud Run/GKE. FirestoreSessionStore lets multiple instances read/write same session via Firestore concurrency. For Postgres-backed Store, you handle locking. No leader election, no cross-instance coordination.

All N workers point to same Postgres PostgresSaver; thread_id is partition key. Pregel loop on any worker replays from persisted checkpoint. Inside langgraph_api: run queue serializes work per thread via multitask strategy. OSS: BYO queue but checkpointer is first-class.

BYO in OSS framework: serialize Context (ctx.to_dict()) and stash in your store (Postgres/Redis), rehydrate on next request from any worker. llama_deploy provides hosted control-plane + queue but is separate repo.

Stateless workers share storage backend; no leader election. Resumable streams let any worker pick up in-progress run because workflow snapshot lives in storage. Suspended HITL state durable via workflow snapshots.

AgentSessionStore abstraction allows N pods to share Cosmos/Redis. CosmosCheckpointStorage and CosmosChatHistoryProvider designed for this. DurableTask provides leader-elected, queue-backed orchestration. Both stateless+shared-store and durable orchestrator paths supported.

Stateless: as long as session state lives in external store (custom Session impl backed by Postgres/Redis), any number of pods serve same session pool. No leader election. RunState.toString/fromString serializes paused run to any KV store. nextjs example uses generic db().set.

Stateless workers + shared store. 10 session backends (SQLAlchemy, Redis, MongoDB, Dapr, OpenAIConversations) live in shared external store. Sticky routing not required if store is consistent. No leader election or centralized run scheduler. Some OpenAI conversation-lock retry logic only.

Stateless: N Python workers all serve same logical Agent instance; user owns message_history storage (DB/Redis/file) and re-passes per request. Durable execution via Temporal/DBOS/Prefect provides per-workflow horizontal recovery.
Not provided by Rig itself. Multi-pod scaling is responsibility of caller's deployment (e.g., axum behind LB); shared state goes through whatever ConversationMemory backend you ship.

Stateless workers: keep Agent instances ephemeral and rehydrate from shared SessionRepository. SDK ships FileSessionManager, S3SessionManager, RepositorySessionManager. No leader election or cluster-aware coordination - SDK is unopinionated.

No leader election, no built-in shared state. Horizontal scaling means N stateless Node processes behind LB, each loading session state from S3Storage (or other SnapshotStorage) on demand. No worker registration/heartbeat/queue.

Standard stateless-worker model: N Node processes (Next.js/Fargate/Cloud Run/Vercel Functions), each pulls session state from shared store (Postgres/Redis/S3/Blob). No leader election, no shared in-memory map. Canonical durable-stream pattern via resumable-stream + Redis.

First-party Pub/Sub and Eventarc trigger controllers in REST server, with semaphore concurrency limiter and exponential-backoff retries (RetriableRunner). Long-running tools supported via IsLongRunning() pause/resume. No in-box cron; wire Cloud Scheduler -> Pub/Sub -> ADK trigger.

First-party: ScheduleManager + SchedulePoller + ScheduleExecutor (croniter-driven) with DB-stored cron schedules. Background agent runs via arun(background=True) produce resumable SSE streams with /resume endpoint. FastAPI BackgroundTasks for hooks. Memory tasks spawned in threads/asyncio.
Not provided. No cron, no schedulers, no webhook receivers. Long-running background work via your own tokio::spawn through Topic<Task>. No first-party primitive.
Not provided as host-level scheduler. AgentDefinition.background:bool is only a sub-agent hint for the CLI. No cron, no webhook trigger, no agent-as-background-worker primitive.

Background sub-agents via AgentDefinition.background and AgentInput.run_in_background (parent turn completes immediately, task_notification fires on completion). Background Bash with run_in_background. AssistantWorkerOptions.scheduling.dir polls scheduled_tasks.json every 10s - local-only filesystem cron, not distributed.

OSS: BYO entirely - kickoff() is blocking, nothing schedules anything. AMP (commercial): first-party Automations + Triggers (Gmail, Calendar, Drive, Outlook, HubSpot, Salesforce, Slack, Zapier, Webhook, Cron). Vendor-managed; no equivalent in OSS repo.
Not provided. No cron, no webhook trigger system, no scheduled-job framework. Use Go stdlib time.AfterFunc/Ticker or a job library (Asynq, Temporal, Cloud Tasks) in your host.

BackgroundModel abstraction and GenerateOperation for long-running model ops (video/Imagen) - poll with CheckModelOperation; for model calls only, not general tasks. Durable streaming via StreamManager (experimental) keeps flows running across HTTP client disconnect. Cron/webhooks BYO.

Pure OSS: not provided - BYO Celery/arq/Temporal/cron. LangGraph Platform (closed-source): ships crons (crons.create/search/delete) and webhooks (run create accepts webhook URL). Platform queue persists scheduled runs in Postgres.
Not provided - BYO (Celery, Temporal, RQ, your own asyncio task).

Three first-party mechanisms: schedulers (Mastra({scheduler}) with cron-like jobs, /api/scheduled-jobs routes), background tasks (disableBackgroundTasks flag, backgroundTaskCheckStep, dedicated chunk family), webhooks/channels (channels/slack, channels/discord packages wire agents into chat events).

Cron/trigger BYO via Azure Functions hosting (Timer/HTTP/MCPTool triggers). Long-running background via Microsoft.Agents.AI.DurableTask treats each agent run as durable orchestration with replay-on-crash. Python equivalent in agent-framework-durabletask (beta).
Not provided. No cron, no webhook trigger primitives, no queues. Run a worker process (BullMQ, AWS SQS, etc.) and call run() from inside it.

Not provided - BYO. No scheduler, no cron, no webhook trigger, no long-running background-agent runtime. Optional temporal extra integrates Temporal workflows for durable orchestration but is separate runtime you stand up. Report flags this as biggest architectural gap.
Not provided directly - BYO via Temporal scheduling, Prefect deployments, DBOS workflows, or any external scheduler. The framework only provides the agent runtime.
Not provided. No cron, no webhook trigger, no background agent. Tokio runtime can spawn your own tasks but Rig offers no scheduling abstraction.
Not provided - BYO. Library is invocation-driven; nothing schedules cron or webhook triggers. (strands-agents-tools ships cron.py as a tool the agent uses, but tool-side not runtime-side.)
Not provided - BYO. No cron primitive, no webhook trigger surface. Use BullMQ/Cloudflare Queues/etc. and call agent.invoke() inside the worker handler.
Not provided. No cron, no scheduler, no webhook trigger primitive. Use your host (Vercel Cron, Cloud Scheduler, Trigger.dev) and invoke agent.generate() from there.

Triggers ship a semaphore-based concurrency limiter (MaxConcurrentRuns) - a thin worker pool. Beyond this, runtime assumes short-lived HTTP request scope. Long runs require IsLongRunning() tools or fire-and-forget Pub/Sub trigger pattern.

No first-party in-process queue (no Celery integration). Scheduler is DB-polling. Long-running runs supported via background=True for fire-and-forget with /resume, or schedules for cron-driven runs. BYO Celery/RQ/Arq for richer queue.
Not provided. Tasks delivered to actors via actor_ref.cast(). No durable queue, no retry semantics at queue layer (only LLM-level retries in optim::RetryLayer).
Not provided - BYO. Runtime model is one CLI subprocess per active session. For queue-shaped workloads, layer your own (Celery, RQ, Temporal, AWS SQS).

Not provided - BYO. Query interface includes streamInput() and stopTask() which give primitives for long-running streaming session, but no shipped queue, no enqueue() API, no leasing semantics. Build on top with BullMQ/Cloud Tasks.
OSS: none. AMP: implicit - each Automation is a separate managed deployment that receives trigger events and runs the crew. No explicit queue API in OSS.

Not provided. Framework assumes short-lived calls into Runner.Run from your HTTP handler. Long-running background work is your responsibility (typical pattern: enqueue, then worker pool calls Runner.Run).

Not provided - BYO. No built-in job queue. Expected model is HTTP request -> run flow synchronously -> respond. For async work, put request on Pub/Sub/SQS/etc. yourself and have separate worker call genkit.Generate on dequeue.

Inside langgraph_api (Platform, closed-source): Postgres-backed work queue with one logical lane per thread_id. Long-running runs are default expectation, with re-attaching client picking up via stream_resumable. OSS: no queue - short-lived HTTP scope unless wrapped.
Not provided - BYO. llama_deploy provides this in a separate project.

Not first-party. Mastra assumes you put it behind normal Node/Edge HTTP infra. pubsub/ directory contains internal pub/sub abstraction but for production queues you bring your own (BullMQ, SQS, etc.).

DurableTask is the explicit queue/orchestrator model (DurableAIAgent, AgentEntity with EntityAgentWrapper). Azure Functions triggers fan out to worker pool. Vanilla in-process agent does not expose queue API but the dedicated path is first-class.
Not provided. SDK assumes short-lived HTTP request scope by default. Long-running agents need serialized RunState checkpoint pattern (HITL example).

Not provided. SDK assumes you embed loop in your own HTTP request scope (or any async task). No internal task queue, no worker pool. For long-running agents: expose streaming endpoint over run_streamed() or persist RunState.to_json() and resume via Celery/RQ/SQS.
No built-in queue. ThreadExecutor lets you supply your own concurrent.futures.Executor for sync tool functions in long-running servers. Otherwise short-lived HTTP request scope assumed.
Not provided. Harness assumes short-lived agent.prompt().await usage. No queue, no worker pool. Long-running runs can stream via agent.stream_prompt() to keep client connected.
Not provided - BYO. ConcurrentToolExecutor parallelizes tool calls within one cycle, but no inter-session queue.
Not provided - BYO. SDK assumes you wrap agent.stream() in your host's request-scoped wrapper. Lone exception is optional A2AExpressServer which assumes one-task-at-a-time per TaskStore.

Not provided - BYO. No queue. SDK assumes request scope. The new @ai-sdk/workflow package adds WorkflowAgent stepped-workflow abstraction wrapping streamText with serializable step IO, but is not a horizontal multi-tenant runtime.
